summary: Gives an overview of the InfiniBand architecture, a high-speed channel-based interconnect between systems and devices. It then describes requirements and guidelines for transmitting IP over InfiniBand, for both IPv4 and IPv6. The document is informational.

eli5.summary: A tour of a very fast road for connecting computers, and a list of what is needed to run ordinary internet traffic on it.

questions: why does ipoib use unreliable datagram
what is an infiniband subnet manager
subtitle: A tour of InfiniBand and the ground rules for running IPv4 and IPv6 over it.

tldr.problem: InfiniBand is a switched fabric with its own addressing, partitions and multicast machinery, so IP cannot simply be dropped onto it without knowing how it works.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes the InfiniBand architecture, then explains how an IP subnet is overlaid on an IB subnet: Unreliable Datagram mode is the data service, one IB broadcast group defines the IP link, and IP multicast maps onto IB multicast groups.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational overview. The encapsulation and address resolution are left to other documents such as RFC 4391.

today: RFC 4392 is an Informational RFC from April 2006 and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an architecture overview; the encapsulation itself is in RFC 4391.

sections.title: How InfiniBand Is Built
sections.content:
The InfiniBand Architecture (IBA) defines a System Area Network that connects processor nodes, I/O platforms and I/O devices through a fabric of cascaded switches and IB routers. Each unit attaches through channel adapters (CAs), and each CA has one or more ports. A port can hold many Queue Pairs (QPs), and the QP number is part of the address for data transfer.

Every IB subnet has at least one subnet manager (SM). It assigns the 16-bit Local Identifier (LID) and the Global Identifier (GID) of each port and programs the switches so packets are routed. The GID is 128 bits: a 64-bit subnet prefix plus a 64-bit EUI-64 part called the GUID. The RFC calls IB routers and subnets by those names so they are not confused with IP routers and subnets.

The RFC also lists the data transfer services: Unreliable Datagram, Reliable Datagram, Reliable Connected, Unreliable Connected, Raw Ethertype and Raw IPv6. Other features it describes are 16 virtual lanes, 16 service levels, partition keys (P_Keys) for isolation and Q_Keys for access rights.
sections.eli5: InfiniBand is like a big building where a manager hands out room numbers and decides which hallways everyone uses. Every computer plugs in through a door with its own mailboxes.

sections.title: InfiniBand Addresses and Multicast Groups
sections.content:
IBA borrows heavily from IPv6 for its GIDs. Unicast GIDs have link-local (FE80/10), site-local (FEC0/10) and global scopes. Multicast GIDs look like FFxy:<112 bits>, where the flag bits are 000T and T=1 marks a transient group.

Multicast groups are managed by the subnet manager. There is no create command: the first join request with the FullMember bit set creates the group, and the last FullMember leaving lets the SM delete it. Other join states are NonMember and SendOnlyNonMember. The SM assigns the group a Multicast LID (MLID), which switches use for routing. Ports can ask for reports of group creation and deletion, sent as traps 66 and 67.
sections.eli5: A multicast group is like a club. You have to tell the manager you want to join, and the club closes when its last real member walks out.

sections.title: Choosing IB as the Data Link
sections.content:
IPoIB could in principle run over any of the IB services. The RFC reasons that only Unreliable Datagram (UD) mode is required on every IB node, supports multicast and has the stronger 32-bit CRC. The Raw Datagram modes are optional and use a 16-bit CRC. UD is therefore the obvious choice, as specified in RFC 4391. The connected modes could be considered in future documents because they allow a larger MTU than UD.

IPoIB must not require changes to IP or higher-layer protocols. Because IP multicast is a basic need, IPoIB requires multicast-capable IB fabrics. Every IPoIB multicast GID sets the transient bit, so IP mappings never collide with IB's well-known Raw Datagram groups.

Spanning one IP subnet across several IB subnets is not possible yet. It would need multicast GIDs that span IB subnets, an IB routing protocol and protocols between IB nodes and IB routers.
sections.eli5: There are several ways to send messages on InfiniBand. The simple postcard-style one works everywhere and can reach many people at once, so it is the one picked for internet traffic.

sections.title: Bringing Up an IPoIB Subnet and Using Multicast
sections.content:
The IPoIB subnet is overlaid on the IB subnet in steps. The administrator creates the all-IPoIB-nodes broadcast group, or it is created by the first join. Each IPoIB interface then joins it as a FullMember. That join also hands the node parameters such as the Q_Key and path MTU. If a port cannot support the group's parameters, the join fails and the port is not part of the IPoIB subnet.

An IP subnet has only one P_Key. Each distinct broadcast group MGID creates a separate abstract link, which is an IPoIB VLAN.

To send IP multicast, the driver should join the matching IB group, either as a FullMember or as a SendOnlyNonMember. To receive, the host must join the group and leave when the IP layer stops listening. Routers have no promiscuous mode, so they ask the SM to report all group creations and join them, ideally as NonMember so their join does not keep the group alive.
sections.eli5: To get onto the IP club's hallway, every computer first joins one big everyone group. Anyone who wants a smaller group has to sign up for it, because nobody can listen to everything.

sections.title: RARP, DHCP and Quality of Service
sections.content:
The IPoIB link-layer address is built from the GID and the Queue Pair Number (QPN). Since the QPN might change across reboots or interface resets, static ARP entries and RARP server entries only work if an implementation keeps the QPN invariant.

DHCPv4 expects a 16-octet client identifier, but an IPoIB address is 20 octets. IPoIB works around this by having the client use the broadcast flag when requesting an address, as specified in RFC 4390.

For quality of service, IB offers service levels, but each IPoIB implementation chooses its own SL by its own policy, and no method is defined by the IPoIB standards.
sections.eli5: The computer's address on this network includes a number that can change when it restarts, so old address lists can go stale. Another rule changes how a computer asks for its first address because its label is too long for the usual form.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it describes the IB architecture as relevant to IPoIB and restates issues from other documents. It specifies no requirements and states that it introduces no security issues. IPoIB-related security issues are described in RFC 4391 and RFC 4390.
sections.eli5: This document only explains how things work, so it adds no new risks. The risks that do exist are written up in the companion documents.

items.label: Reliable Connected
items.desc: Acknowledged, one local QP to one remote QP.

items.label: Unreliable Connected
items.desc: Connection oriented with no acknowledgement or resend.

items.label: Raw Ethertype
items.desc: Raw datagram carrying a protocol type.

items.label: Raw IPv6
items.desc: Raw datagram that carries native IPv6 packets.

items.label: FullMember
items.desc: Receives and sends group traffic; the group lives while a FullMember remains.

items.label: NonMember
items.desc: Receives and sends, but does not count for creating or deleting the group.

items.label: SendOnlyNonMember
items.desc: Only sends to the group; does not count for creating or deleting it.
